title: Electrochemical Reactions
standard_text: Galvanic (voltaic) cells and electrolytic cells; the anode (oxidation) and cathode (reduction); the salt bridge; cell notation; standard electrode potentials and E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; electrolysis of copper(II) chloride, the refining of copper, the chlor-alkali industry and the extraction of aluminium. (summary of the senior secondary Chemistry curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Chemistry worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): galvanic cells, standard electrode potentials, electrolytic cells, electrolysis and batteries and corrosion. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Oxidation happens at the anode; reduction at the cathode.
body_html:
How to think about it

A galvanic cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy by a spontaneous redox reaction; an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to cause a non-spontaneous reaction. In both, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The salt bridge keeps the solutions neutral by letting ions move.

From the table of standard reduction potentials, the half-cell with the higher E° is reduced (cathode). A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous. Electrolysis is used to refine copper, to make chlorine and sodium hydroxide from brine (chlor-alkali), and to extract aluminium from bauxite.

Example

Zn²⁺/Zn −0.76 V; Cu²⁺/Cu +0.34 V. E°cell?

Cu is the cathode.

Answer: +1.10 V

Example

In a galvanic cell, which electrode is negative?

Electrons leave it.

Answer: the anode

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the anode is always positive.
  • Subtracting E° values the wrong way round.
  • Thinking electrons flow through the salt bridge.

items.q: Which product forms at the negative electrode (cathode) during electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (brine)?
